READING

**The rent arithmetic, in full**

Ardenshaw locks in £214,000 a year for ten years from 2027-11-30: £2,140,000 in total rent.

Kesterwick costs:
- Non-refundable deposit: £40,000
- Works: £480,000
- Culverstone rent: £118,000 × 10 = £1,180,000
- Dead mileage penalty (see below): ~£25,900 × 10 = £259,000
- Worst-case Nethercote bridging (see below): ~£74,000

Worst-case Kesterwick total: approximately £2,033,000

Ardenshaw is more expensive in every scenario, by roughly £107,000 at worst and £181,000 at best. The capital outlay of £520,000 (deposit + works) is recovered through rent savings in about 7.4 years; years eight through ten are clear. That is the foundation.

**Dead mileage, worked**

Culverstone is three miles further from the 44 stand at Verrancombe Bridge. Each vehicle makes at least one outward and one return movement per day, so the incremental dead mileage is 6 miles per vehicle per operating day.

22 vehicles × 313 days × 6 miles × £0.63 = **£25,904 a year**

That is the honest carrying cost of Culverstone's position. It reduces but does not reverse the rent saving: £214,000 − £118,000 − £25,904 = **£70,096 net annual saving** against Ardenshaw.

**Planning timeline: what the numbers actually say**

Application validated: 2026-08-14.

| Scenario | Weeks from validation | Consent date | + 22 weeks works | Hallowbrand ends | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Target | 13 | 2026-11-13 | 2027-04-08 | 2027-11-30 | None |
| Median | 34 | 2027-04-08 | 2027-09-10 | 2027-11-30 | None |
| Break-even | ~42 | 2027-06-04 | 2027-10-30 | 2027-11-30 | ~1 month |
| Worst recorded | 61 | 2027-10-15 | 2028-03-18 | 2027-11-30 | ~3.5 months |

The median result delivers Culverstone roughly two months before the Hallowbrand lease expires. There is no gap. A gap only materialises if processing runs beyond about 42 weeks — the slower half of the historical tail.

**Worst-case gap: what it actually costs**

If processing hits 61 weeks and works follow, Nethercote is needed from approximately December 2027 to mid-March 2028: roughly 3.5 months.

£18,500 × 3.5 ≈ **£64,750** — call it £74,000 to be conservative.

That is the price of the worst outcome the county has ever produced. It is real money but it is a fraction of the rent differential and it does not reverse the overall calculation.

**The workshop gap is a genuine operational risk, not a financial one**

Four months at Nethercote with no workshop means maintenance must be contracted out or done by mobile engineers. For a 31-vehicle fleet running a tendered network and school contracts, this is demanding but not exotic. Many operators maintain fleets through third-party facilities during depot moves. It is a management problem, not a structural failure. The business holds the full 44 and 44A contract through 2028-03-31, so the operational requirement is clear and not seasonal.

**Cash position**

Current: £640,000 cash, £200,000 undrawn facility = £840,000 headroom.

Deposit (December 2026): −£40,000 → £600,000 cash
Works (drawn over 22 weeks, starting at consent): −£480,000 → £120,000 cash, facility intact

The facility was presumably not established to sit permanently undrawn. Drawing part of it to fund a planned capital project is exactly its purpose. After all construction is paid, the business carries £120,000 cash plus £200,000 facility. That is thin for a 31-vehicle operation, but the works spend is complete at that point; there is no ongoing capital commitment, and rent has just dropped by £96,000 a year. Cash rebuilds quickly.

**The 44 bid: 2027-09-14**

Depot cost enters the bid as a fixed line. Under Ardenshaw that line is £214,000. Under Kesterwick it is £118,000 (plus any dead mileage adjustment to operating costs). The £96,000 difference in the fixed line is either passed to the authority as a lower price — improving competitive odds on a tendered contract where price is decisive — or retained as margin. In neither case is a higher number better.

There is a legitimate concern about bidding under Kesterwick if, in the very worst planning scenario, consent has not yet been granted at bid time. In that scenario (consent ~October 2027, bid due September 2027), Culverstone would not yet have been consented. However: the new contract does not commence until April 2028, and even the worst recorded determination plus 22 weeks of works delivers Culverstone in approximately March 2028. The bidder knows their Culverstone cost with certainty — it is £118,000 plus measurable dead mileage — and knows the site will be operational before any obligation under the new contract falls due. The £40,000 deposit holds Faskally's option to June 2028, providing a backstop. The bid can be constructed on solid ground.

**What Ardenshaw actually buys**

Ardenshaw purchases certainty. The certainty it purchases is:
- No gap at Nethercote (worth at most £74,000, the worst-case cost of the gap)
- No workshop interruption (an operational convenience, not a financial saving)
- A known depot cost at bid time (achievable under Kesterwick with slightly more care)

The price of that certainty is £214,000 a year for ten years, versus £143,904 (rent plus dead mileage) under Kesterwick. The premium is approximately £700,000 over the lease term against a net capital outlay of £520,000. That is not a risk premium — it is overpaying by a material amount to avoid a problem that, in the median case, does not arise at all.

**The only scenario that genuinely hurts Kesterwick**

Planning refusal — not delay — would be damaging. The business would have paid £40,000 (non-refundable), let Hallowbrand lapse, and have no depot from December 2027. The problem statement gives no indication that refusal is the expected outcome: the application has been validated, which is a substantive threshold, and the county's own record of 13-to-61-week determinations implies a pattern of approvals rather than refusals. This risk exists and should be monitored, but it is not the question before us; the question is which course to recommend given the information provided, and planning delay — not refusal — is the identified risk.

**Against BALANCED**

BALANCED is appropriate when the two options are genuinely even. They are not. The 10-year numbers favour Kesterwick in every scenario I can construct. The operational risks are real but bounded. The bid question is answerable. This is a case where uncertainty around timing is being mistaken for uncertainty around outcome: the outcome, financially, is clear.

---

READING
Kesterwick's ten-year cost comes in below Ardenshaw's even when every adverse assumption is stacked — worst-recorded planning timeline, full Nethercote bridging, full dead mileage carried throughout. The net annual saving after dead mileage is £70,096; the capital outlay of £520,000 pays back in under eight years; the deposit-extended Faskally option holds the site past the date the new 44 contract commences; and the lower depot cost line strengthens a bid on which the business's core revenue depends. The maximum extra cost of the worst-case Nethercote gap is approximately £74,000 — less than thirteen months of the rent differential — and the workshop interruption it entails is an operational management problem, not an insuperable one. Ardenshaw's premium purchases certainty that the planning timeline does not, in probability-weighted terms, justify paying for.

CALL
KESTERWICK

GROUNDS
The ten-year arithmetic favours Culverstone in every scenario constructed, including the worst planning outcome the county has ever recorded, and the deposit-secured option holds the site past the new contract commencement date, meaning the certainty premium demanded by Ardenshaw is not warranted by any of the identified risks.
